Newborn Care

Omphalocele: diagnosis, associated conditions and treatment

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Omphalocele, also called exomphalos, is a birth defect at the base of the umbilical cord. Intestine, liver or other organs extend outside the abdomen inside a membrane-covered sac. The diagnosis needs specialist assessment, but it does not give a single prognosis: the organs involved, available abdominal space, lungs and any associated conditions all matter.

What omphalocele is

During normal early development, the intestine temporarily extends into the umbilical cord and returns to the abdomen around the end of the first trimester. With omphalocele, the abdominal wall has not closed normally. An early scan must be interpreted for the exact gestation; normal temporary gut herniation is not automatically a defect.

The covering is a membrane, not normal skin. It is often intact at birth but can rupture. Omphalocele differs from gastroschisis, where bowel usually lies uncovered beside the cord, and from an ordinary childhood umbilical hernia. These conditions have different associated problems and care pathways.

Size, abdominal space and immediate risks

A small defect may contain only some intestine; a large or giant omphalocele may contain much of the liver and other organs. Definitions of giant vary. The important question is whether organs can fit inside safely, not a size label alone.

The abdominal cavity may be too small for immediate closure. A ruptured sac increases infection and protection concerns; trapped or twisted organs can lose blood supply. Giant defects can accompany underdeveloped lungs or pulmonary hypertension. These possibilities need assessment, rather than being inevitable in every baby.

How common it is, and what else may be found

Omphalocele is uncommon. The CDC's April 2026 US surveillance report estimates about 2.7 cases per 10,000 live births, approximately one in 3,704. This population estimate is not a worldwide rate or an individual prediction.

Some babies have an isolated defect; others have heart, brain or spinal, gastrointestinal, urinary or chromosome conditions. Trisomies 13 and 18 and Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum are examples considered during assessment. An associated condition is not certain, and apparently isolated findings before birth may need reassessment afterwards.

Causes and risk-factor evidence without blame

The cause is unknown in many cases. Genetic or chromosome changes can contribute, sometimes within a syndrome. No single food, drink or everyday action can usually be identified as the cause in an individual pregnancy. A diagnosis is not proof that a parent caused it.

Older observational studies reported associations with alcohol, heavy smoking, prepregnancy obesity and some SSRI antidepressant exposures. These studies do not prove individual causation or an identical effect for every medicine. Later SSRI analyses did not confirm every earlier signal. Review medicines with the prescriber; do not stop or switch an antidepressant on your own. Seek support to avoid alcohol and tobacco and manage existing health conditions, without assuming all birth defects can be prevented.

Prenatal diagnosis and further tests

An abnormal maternal serum screening result can raise concern but cannot diagnose omphalocele. Expert ultrasound assesses the abdominal wall, organs in the sac, growth and other anatomy. Detailed heart assessment, often fetal echocardiography, and sometimes MRI help plan care. Measurements inform counselling but do not determine the outcome alone.

Discuss diagnostic genetic testing, including sampling options and chromosome analysis or microarray, with the fetal and genetic teams. The 2026 ERNICA guideline also suggests offering exome, or available genome, sequencing after counselling. These are choices, not mandatory tests. No test excludes every syndrome; suspected Beckwith–Wiedemann spectrum may need a specific testing approach beyond routine chromosome or sequencing results.

Planning birth and recognizing the defect afterwards

The team plans monitoring, delivery location and access to neonatal surgery, with transfer arrangements if needed. Vaginal birth is generally suitable for non-giant omphalocele unless there is another obstetric reason for caesarean. Large liver-containing defects need an individual birth plan. A caesarean is neither required for all cases nor a guarantee against complications.

Some cases are first recognized at birth. A visible sac containing organs requires immediate neonatal assessment, even if the baby seems comfortable. Staff protect the sac, maintain warmth and fluids, assess breathing and circulation and look for other conditions. Do not push the organs in, puncture the sac or improvise dressings or creams.

Primary repair: one operation when safe

Treatment depends on size, liver involvement, abdominal capacity, gestational age, breathing and associated conditions. A small defect may be repaired soon after birth by returning the organs and closing the wall, sometimes with a patch. The baby must be assessed and stable enough first.

Immediate specialist care does not mean every intact small defect needs emergency surgery within a fixed number of hours. The 2026 ERNICA guideline bases timing for non-giant, non-ruptured defects on the baby's condition and an experienced surgical team. Rupture, threatened organs or other complications can change the urgency.

Staged reduction and delayed closure

For a large defect, forcing the organs into a tight abdomen can impair breathing or circulation. In staged repair, the surgical team uses a protective covering or silo and gradually returns the contents before closure. Technique, pain control and breathing support are chosen individually; not every baby needs the same ventilation plan.

Another option for selected giant defects is non-operative sac care while skin grows over it, followed by later abdominal-wall repair. The 2026 European guideline conditionally suggests delayed closure after the first birthday following this approach; evidence is limited and timing remains individual. This is active supervised care, not leaving the condition untreated. Use only the team's prescribed dressing plan: household honey, iodine, silver products or other creams are not DIY alternatives. Home care is possible only when the team has trained the family and arranged follow-up.

Feeding, recovery and longer-term needs

Some babies need intravenous nutrition, tube feeds or respiratory support. Feeding depends on bowel function, stability and treatment: selected babies undergoing staged reduction may start small enteral feeds before final closure. Do not assume every baby must wait for closure, or start or change feeds without the team.

Recovery can involve reflux, feeding difficulty, slow growth, wound or later hernia problems and, especially with giant defects, continuing breathing or developmental needs. Follow-up may include surgery, paediatrics, nutrition and developmental support, with diagnosis-specific care for associated conditions. Survival, hospital stay and future needs cannot be promised from one size or an online percentage.

Questions, future pregnancies and support

Ask which organs are involved, whether the sac is intact, what additional findings need investigation and why a particular repair strategy is recommended. Before discharge obtain written feeding, wound or sac-care instructions, medicines, emergency contacts and follow-up dates. Ask how results will be explained and what practical or emotional support is available.

Recurrence advice depends on whether a genetic cause is identified and on family history. Genetic counselling can explain this before another pregnancy. Routine prenatal care, medication review and support for health needs are useful, but do not guarantee prevention or require blame or self-directed treatment changes.

When to get immediate help

Alert the hospital team immediately if the sac tears, leaks, bleeds or changes colour, or the baby deteriorates. Outside hospital seek immediate emergency care for breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor, floppiness, difficulty waking, unresponsiveness, a seizure or green vomit. A baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher, or a temperature below 36°C, also needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to drive or call an ambulance.

Contact the treating team promptly for worsening feeding, repeated vomiting, increasing abdominal swelling, wound redness, discharge or poor weight gain; follow any stricter individual instructions. Do not wait for the next routine visit if something is wrong, or assume every new symptom is ordinary reflux. Never squeeze or attempt to reduce a bulge yourself.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the fetal and genetic teams to explain the anatomy, associated findings, test choices and limitations, and the birth and transfer plan.

Discuss why primary, staged or delayed closure is proposed, how comfort, breathing and feeding will be managed, and what changes require urgent contact.

Practise only prescribed wound, sac or equipment care with the team; obtain written home instructions and keep follow-up, without DIY reduction or medicine changes.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help record questions, results to discuss, appointments and feeding or symptom observations. It cannot diagnose the defect, interpret genetic results, judge whether a sac is safe or change dressings, feeds or medicines. Seek care for warnings regardless of the app record.

When to seek help

Seek immediate help for sac rupture, leakage, bleeding or colour change, or a deteriorating baby. Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor, floppiness, difficulty waking, unresponsiveness, seizure or green vomit needs emergency care. Under 3 months, a temperature of 38°C or higher, or below 36°C, needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself; ask another driver or call an ambulance. Follow the individual plan; do not push organs in, puncture a sac or improvise products, feeds or medicine changes.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Omphalocele is a sac-covered defect at the umbilical cord, distinct from gastroschisis and an ordinary umbilical hernia.
  • Size, abdominal capacity, lungs, genetics and associated conditions guide counselling and treatment.
  • Historical exposure associations do not identify a parent's actions as the cause; medicines need prescriber review, not abrupt stopping.
  • Primary, staged and supervised delayed repair are different options; timing and feeding plans are individual.
  • Newborn deterioration, green vomit or a damaged sac needs immediate help; follow the team's written plan.

Frequently asked questions

What causes omphalocele?

Often no single cause is known. Some cases involve chromosome or gene changes or a wider syndrome. An individual diagnosis does not show that a particular food, medicine or action caused it. Genetic counselling can clarify findings and recurrence.

Which factors have been associated with it?

Older studies reported alcohol, heavy smoking, prepregnancy obesity and some SSRI associations, with important confounding and small-number limits. Association is not individual causation. Do not stop an antidepressant yourself; review its benefits and risks with the prescriber and seek support for health needs.

How is it diagnosed during pregnancy?

An abnormal serum screen may raise concern, but expert ultrasound identifies the structural finding. Heart assessment and selected MRI or diagnostic genetic tests may add information. Counselling should explain what tests can and cannot detect; a screening result is not a diagnosis.

Can it be treated?

Yes, specialist care can include one-stage repair, staged reduction or supervised sac care followed by delayed closure. The safest choice depends on the baby and associated conditions. Prompt newborn care does not mean every stable intact defect needs an emergency operation or the same timetable.

Is the sac strong enough to protect the organs?

It is a thin membrane, not skin, and can rupture. The neonatal team protects it and checks the organs and circulation. Do not puncture it, push organs back or apply an improvised product. Report tears, leakage, bleeding or colour changes immediately.

Will a caesarean be necessary?

Not automatically. Vaginal delivery is generally appropriate for non-giant defects unless obstetric factors require otherwise. A giant or liver-containing omphalocele needs an individual plan with fetal medicine, neonatology and surgery.

What can recovery involve?

Breathing support, intravenous or tube nutrition and gradual milk feeding may be needed. Some selected babies can start small enteral feeds during staged treatment. Growth, reflux, breathing, development and later hernia follow-up vary; a single outcome cannot be guaranteed.

What needs emergency help after discharge?

Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, unusual pallor, floppiness, difficulty waking, unresponsiveness, a seizure or green vomit need immediate emergency care. Under 3 months, 38°C or higher, or a temperature below 36°C, also needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not drive yourself; ask another driver or call an ambulance. Contact the team immediately for a damaged or changed sac and follow the individual emergency plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
